parts.label: b
parts.question: Is the argument $p\to q,\ q\ \therefore p$ valid? Justify using the definition of validity.
parts.solution: Invalid. Take $p=F,q=T$. Then $p\to q=T$ and $q=T$, but $p=F$. Thus all premises can be true while the conclusion is false.

parts.label: a
parts.question: For sets $A,B,C$, prove $(A\setminus B)\cap C=A\cap(C\setminus B)$ by element membership.
parts.solution: For any $x$, $x\in(A\setminus B)\cap C$ iff $x\in A$, $x\notin B$, and $x\in C$; these are exactly the conditions for $x\in A\cap(C\setminus B)$. Thus the sets have the same elements.
parts.rubric: 1 correct membership conditions; 1 both directions/equality.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Let $O=\{2k+1:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ and $f:\mathbb Z\to O$, $f(k)=2k+1$. Prove $f$ is bijective and give its inverse with domain and codomain.
parts.solution: If $2a+1=2b+1$, then $a=b$, so $f$ is injective. Every $y\in O$ has the form $2k+1$, so $f(k)=y$; hence $f$ is onto. Its inverse is $f^{-1}:O\to\mathbb Z$, $f^{-1}(y)=(y-1)/2$, which is an integer for all $y\in O$.
parts.rubric: 1 injection; 1 surjection; 1 inverse and correct domains.

parts.question: Construct a complete truth table for $(p\oplus q)\leftrightarrow\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)$. Classify it as a tautology, contradiction, or contingency.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Use contraposition to prove: for positive real numbers $a,b,c$, if $ab\le c^2$, then $a\le c$ or $b\le c$. State the contrapositive explicitly.
parts.solution: The contrapositive is: if $a>c$ and $b>c$, then $ab>c^2$. Assuming both inequalities, positivity gives $ab>cb>c^2$. This proves the contrapositive and therefore the original implication. Negating the disjunction requires both strict inequalities.
parts.rubric: 2 correct contrapositive including conjunction; 2 product inequalities using positivity; 1 conclusion via contraposition.

parts.label: a
parts.question: The domain is all employees. $M(x,y)$ means $y$ mentors $x$. Translate: (i) every employee has exactly one mentor; (ii) there is exactly one employee who mentors everyone. Each is worth 2 points.
parts.solution: (i) $\forall x\exists y(M(x,y)\land\forall z(M(x,z)\to z=y))$. (ii) $\exists y(\forall x M(x,y)\land\forall z((\forall x M(x,z))\to z=y))$. The first permits different unique mentors for different employees; the second identifies one unique universal mentor.
parts.rubric: 2 each: existence and intended quantifier order (1), uniqueness with correct predicate (1).

parts.label: b
parts.question: Prove $(\forall x P(x))\lor(\forall x Q(x))\Rightarrow\forall x(P(x)\lor Q(x))$. Give a two-element countermodel to the reverse implication.
parts.solution: If all elements satisfy $P$, every element satisfies $P\lor Q$; the same holds if all satisfy $Q$. For the reverse take $D=\{a,b\}$ with $P(a)=T,P(b)=F,Q(a)=F,Q(b)=T$. Every element satisfies the disjunction, but neither predicate holds universally.
parts.rubric: 2 valid forward reasoning; 1 predicate table; 1 checking reverse premise true/conclusion false.

parts.label: c
parts.question: From $\forall x(P(x)\to Q(x))$ and $\forall x(Q(x)\to R(x))$, derive $\forall x(P(x)\to R(x))$. Name the inference rules and explain why generalization is allowed.
parts.solution: Let $a$ be arbitrary. Universal instantiation yields $P(a)\to Q(a)$ and $Q(a)\to R(a)$. Hypothetical syllogism gives $P(a)\to R(a)$. Since $a$ was arbitrary and no premise singles it out, universal generalization yields the conclusion.
parts.rubric: 1 arbitrary element; 2 universal instantiations; 1 hypothetical syllogism; 1 justified universal generalization.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Let $S=\{\varnothing,\{1\}\}$. List $\mathcal P(S)$ and find its cardinality.
parts.solution: \[\mathcal P(S)=\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\},\{\{1\}\},\{\varnothing,\{1\}\}\}.\] There are four subsets. The two elements of $S$ are themselves distinct sets.
parts.rubric: 1 complete correct roster; 1 cardinality and correct nesting.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Let $f,g:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ satisfy $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=-x$. Compute $f\circ g$ and $g\circ f$, and determine whether the two compositions are equal.
parts.solution: $(f\circ g)(x)=1-x$ and $(g\circ f)(x)=-x-1$. Their values differ by 2 for every integer input, so the functions are unequal. Both have domain and codomain $\mathbb Z$.
parts.rubric: 1 each composition; 1 non-equality with a valid comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Give direct proofs: (i) the product of two rational numbers is rational (3 points); (ii) the product of two integer perfect squares is a perfect square (2 points). Use the definitions.
parts.solution: (i) Write $u=a/b$ and $v=c/d$ with integers $a,b,c,d$ and $b,d\ne0$. Then $uv=ac/(bd)$; $ac,bd$ are integers and $bd\ne0$, so the product is rational. Each is worth 2 points.

parts.label: a
parts.question: For $f:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, $f(x)=x^2$, determine whether an inverse function on the stated codomain exists. Explain.
parts.solution: No. It is onto $[0,\infty)$, since $y\ge0$ has preimage $\sqrt y$, but it is not injective: $f(1)=f(-1)=1$. An inverse would have to return two different preimages for 1, violating uniqueness.
parts.rubric: 1 correct noninjectivity example; 1 no inverse and uniqueness explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.question: For any set $S$, show that no function $h:S\to\mathcal P(S)$ is onto, using $D=\{x\in S:x\notin h(x)\}$. Deduce $|S|<|\mathcal P(S)|$.
parts.solution: $D\subseteq S$, so $D\in\mathcal P(S)$. If $h(a)=D$, then $a\in D$ iff $a\notin h(a)$ iff $a\notin D$, a contradiction. Thus $D$ is missed. The singleton map $x\mapsto\{x\}$ is injective, but no bijection exists because no map $S\to\mathcal P(S)$ is onto. Hence the strict inequality.
parts.rubric: 1 diagonal subset lies in codomain; 1 contradiction for any proposed preimage; 1 singleton injection and strict inequality.

parts.question: Classify each formula as a tautology, contradiction, or contingency, with brief justification: (i) $(p\land q)\to p$; (ii) $(p\to q)\land p\land\neg q$; (iii) $p\leftrightarrow\neg q$. Each is worth 1 point.
parts.solution: (i) Tautology: a true conjunction has $p$ true, and a false antecedent makes the implication true. (ii) Contradiction: $p\land\neg q$ makes $p\to q$ false. (iii) Contingency: true at $p=T,q=F$, false at $p=q=T$.
parts.rubric: 1 each correct classification supported by valid reasoning.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Each of A and B is either a knight (always truthful) or a knave (always lying). A says, \emph{B is a knight}. B says, \emph{We are of different types}. Determine both types and justify.
parts.solution: Let $p,q$ mean that A,B are knights. Consistency requires $p\leftrightarrow q$ and $q\leftrightarrow(p\oplus q)$. The first forces $p=q$, making the XOR false; hence $q=F$ and $p=F$. Both are knaves; both assertions are false.
parts.rubric: 1 consistent equations/reasoning; 1 unique types with verification.

parts.question: In $(\forall x(P(x,y)\to\exists y\,R(x,y)))\land Q(y)$, identify every free and bound variable occurrence and each quantifier\textquotesingle s scope (3 points). Rename the inner bound variable to remove the repeated name, preserving meaning (1 point).

The $y$ in $P(x,y)$ and in $Q(y)$ are free; the $y$ in $R(x,y)$ is bound by $\exists y$, whose scope is $R(x,y)$. Thus this is open in $y$. A renaming is $(\forall x(P(x,y)\to\exists z\,R(x,z)))\land Q(y)$, with fresh $z$.
parts.rubric: 1 x occurrences/scope; 1 y bound occurrence/scope; 1 free occurrences/open status; 1 capture-free renaming.

The original is true because its antecedent is false. The proposed universal formula fails at $x=a$ for every $y$.
parts.rubric: 1 antecedent negation/polarity flip; 1 correctly moved quantifiers; 1 countermodel; 1 both formula values.

Finally existentially generalize in the first coordinate. The witness $a$ is particular and is never universally generalized.
parts.rubric: 1 fresh a; 1 arbitrary b; 1 instantiations/MP; 1 valid universal generalization of b; 1 existential generalization of a.

parts.question: Let $A=\{0,1\}$, $B=\{a\}$. List $A\times B$ and give a relation from $A$ to $B$ which is not a function $A\to B$.

parts.rubric: 1 correct product; 1 valid relation with missing-output explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Use the Schr\"oder--Bernstein theorem to show $|(0,1)|=|[0,1]|$. State the theorem and exhibit both injections; do not prove the theorem.

parts.rubric: 1 theorem; 1 inclusion; 1 valid reverse injection and conclusion.

Each item is worth 1 point.\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]\item $A\cap(A\cup B)=A$ for all sets $A,B$.\item $U\setminus(A\cup B)=(U\setminus A)\cup(U\setminus B)$ for all $A,B\subseteq U$.\item If finite $A,B$ are disjoint, then $|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|$.\item $(a,b)=(b,a)$ for all objects $a,b$.\item If $A\subseteq B$, then $A\setminus B=\varnothing$.\item A one-to-one correspondence means a function that is both injective and surjective.\item An injection from $A$ to $B$ and one from $B$ to $A$ force $|A|=|B|$.\end{enumerate}

parts.question: Let $c$ mean \emph{the battery is charged} and $w$ mean \emph{the device works}. Translate \emph{charging the battery is sufficient for the device to work} and \emph{working is necessary for being charged}. Do these statements rule out $w=T,c=F$?

parts.label: c
parts.question: Let $m$ be a fixed odd integer. Prove that for every integer $n$, $n+m$ is even if and only if $n$ is odd. Prove both directions from the definitions.
parts.solution: Write $m=2h+1$ with $h\in\mathbb Z$. If $n=2k+1$, then $n+m=2(k+h+1)$ is even. Conversely, if $n+m=2t$, then $n=2t-(2h+1)=2(t-h-1)+1$ is odd. Each displayed witness is an integer, and both implications establish the biconditional.
parts.rubric: 1 fixed odd representation; 2 forward definition/witness; 2 reverse definition/witness.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Over $\mathbb R$, evaluate with justification: (i) $\forall x\exists y(y>x)$; (ii) $\exists y\forall x(y>x)$ (1 point each). Explain whether $\forall x\forall yP(x,y)$ and $\forall y\forall xP(x,y)$ are always equivalent (2 points).
parts.solution: (i) True: choose $y=x+1$ for each $x$. (ii) False: for any proposed $y$, take $x=y$, which fails $y>x$. The two universal formulas are equivalent: each requires $P$ at every ordered pair $(x,y)$, so changing traversal order changes no requirement.
parts.rubric: 1 witness; 1 counterexample depending on candidate y; 2 equal-type-order justification.

parts.question: All variables range over $\mathbb R$. Negate $\forall x(x>0\to\exists y(y>0\land\forall z(z>y\to P(x,y,z))))$. Leave no negation before a quantifier or compound formula.

parts.rubric: 1 outer restriction and quantifier; 1 existential-y negation; 1 inner implication and z; 1 correct atomic form/scopes.

parts.question: Prove both equivalences by witness/arbitrary-element reasoning: (i) $\exists x(P(x)\lor Q(x))\equiv(\exists xP(x))\lor(\exists xQ(x))$ (3 points); (ii) $\forall x(P(x)\land Q(x))\equiv(\forall xP(x))\land(\forall xQ(x))$ (2 points).
parts.solution: (i) A witness satisfying $P\lor Q$ satisfies at least one predicate, giving the corresponding existential statement. Conversely, a witness for either existential satisfies the disjunction. (ii) If every element satisfies both predicates, each holds universally. Conversely, if both hold universally, an arbitrary element satisfies both, so their conjunction holds universally.
parts.rubric: (i) 1 forward witness/case reasoning, 2 reverse reasoning and both directions; (ii) 1 each direction with arbitrary elements.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Prove $A\cup(B\setminus A)=A\cup B$ by membership or set laws.
parts.solution: For arbitrary $x$, if $x\in A\cup B$, either $x\in A$, or $x\in B\setminus A$ when $x\notin A$; hence $x$ is in the left set. Conversely, every left-set element lies in $A$ or $B$. Thus both contain the same elements.
parts.rubric: 1 each inclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Describe an enumeration of all positive rationals that lists each rational exactly once. Explain why it reaches every rational and why the set is infinite.
parts.solution: List positive integer pairs $(a,b)$ by increasing $a+b$, breaking ties by $a$. Output $a/b$ only if that value has not appeared earlier. Every positive rational has a positive numerator/denominator representation, whose pair appears in a finite layer, so the rational eventually appears; first-occurrence filtering removes duplicates. The positive integers are distinct positive rationals, so the set is infinite and therefore countably infinite.
parts.rubric: 1 finite diagonal layers; 1 duplicate removal and exhaustive argument; 1 infinitude/classification.

Each assigned output must lie in the stated codomain.\item \textbf{F}. This additional requirement characterizes functions; relations are arbitrary subsets of $A\times B$.\item \textbf{T}. Equal cardinality is defined by existence of a bijection.\end{enumerate}

parts.label: a
parts.question: Simplify $(p\lor(p\land q))\land(q\lor\neg q)\lor(r\land F)$, using the usual precedence. Name the laws used.
parts.solution: Parenthesize as $[(p\lor(p\land q))\land(q\lor\neg q)]\lor(r\land F)$. Absorption gives $p\lor(p\land q)\equiv p$; negation gives $q\lor\neg q\equiv T$; domination gives $r\land F\equiv F$. Identity laws yield $(p\land T)\lor F\equiv\boxed p$.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Let $u$ be rational and $v$ irrational. Prove by contradiction that $u+v$ is irrational. Identify the contradictory conclusions.
parts.solution: Suppose $u+v$ is rational. Write $u=a/b$ and $u+v=c/d$ with integer numerators and nonzero integer denominators. Then $v=(u+v)-u=(bc-ad)/(bd)$ has integer numerator and nonzero integer denominator, so $v$ is rational. This contradicts the given irrationality of $v$, so the assumption was false.
parts.rubric: 1 negated conclusion assumption; 1 two rational representations; 1 valid difference; 1 integer/nonzero conditions; 1 explicit rational/irrational contradiction and conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.question: A function $\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}$ is computable if a finite program returns its value and terminates on every input. Explain why uncomputable functions of this type must exist.
parts.solution: Finite programs are finite strings over a finite alphabet and can be listed by length, so there are at most countably many programs and computable functions. Each binary-valued function corresponds bijectively to the subset $\{n:f(n)=1\}$ of $\mathbb N$; there are uncountably many such subsets by Cantor\textquotesingle s theorem. Countably many programs cannot compute all these functions, so some are uncomputable.
parts.rubric: 1 countability of finite programs; 1 characteristic-function correspondence/uncountability; 1 cardinality comparison and conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.question: For an integer $n$, prove by a cycle of implications that the following are equivalent: (I) $n$ is odd; (II) $n+1$ is even; (III) $n^2$ is odd.
parts.solution: (I)$\Rightarrow$(II): $n=2k+1$ gives $n+1=2(k+1)$. (II)$\Rightarrow$(III): $n+1=2h$ gives $n=2(h-1)+1$, whose square is $2(2(h-1)^2+2(h-1))+1$. parts.rubric: 1 first implication; 2 second implication and integer witnesses; 1 third implication; 1 cycle justifies equivalence.

parts.solution: (i) $\forall x(x\ne0\to\exists y(xy=1))$. (ii) $\exists x(x<0\land x^2=x)$. The correct second formula is false: $x^2=x$ has only roots 0 and 1. The existential implication is true, since $x=2$ makes its antecedent false. It therefore fails to express the required negative-root existence; restricted existence requires a conjunction.
parts.rubric: 1 inverse translation; 1 negative-root translation; 1 false-premise witness for wrong formula; 1 correct-formula falsehood and restriction explanation.

The missing real contradicts completeness of the list.
parts.rubric: 1 construction and interval membership; 1 every row differs; 1 decimal ambiguity and contradiction.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Is the liar sentence \emph{This sentence is false} a proposition under the classical definition used in the lecture (1 point)? If $p\to q$ is given, does that logically assert \emph{$q$ only if $p$} (1 point)? Explain briefly.
parts.solution: The liar sentence is not a proposition: assigning either truth value makes its own assertion inconsistent. The second claim is also false: $q$ only if $p$ means $q\to p$, the converse. $p=F,q=T$ satisfies the given implication but refutes that converse.
parts.rubric: 1 paradox classification/reason; 1 only-if direction and counterassignment.

parts.label: a
parts.question: In $\forall xP(x)\lor Q(x)$, use quantifier precedence to insert parentheses, identify free occurrences and decide whether it is a proposition (2 points). Translate \emph{some real is at least every real} and give its truth value with justification (2 points).
parts.solution: The grouping is $(\forall xP(x))\lor Q(x)$. The $x$ in $P$ is bound and the $x$ in $Q$ is free, so the expression is open and not yet a proposition. The translation is $\exists y\in\mathbb R\,\forall x\in\mathbb R(x\le y)$, false since $x=y+1$ defeats any candidate $y$.
parts.rubric: 2 grouping and free/open status; 1 translation; 1 candidate-dependent counterexample.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Within $U=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}$, let $A=\{0,2,4\}$ and $B=\{2,3,4\}$. Find $A\setminus B$, $U\setminus(A\cup B)$, and $|A\cup B|$, verifying the last value by the two-set identity.
parts.solution: $A\setminus B=\{0\}$ and $U\setminus(A\cup B)=\{1,5\}$. Since $A\cap B=\{2,4\}$, the union size is $3+3-2=4$, agreeing with the roster $\{0,2,3,4\}$.
parts.rubric: 1 both difference/complement rosters; 1 union size with intersection identity.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Construct an explicit bijection $h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ by assigning nonnegative integers to even inputs and negative integers to odd inputs. Prove injectivity and surjectivity.
parts.solution: \[h(n)=\begin{cases}n/2,&n\text{ even},\\-(n+1)/2,&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}\] Each branch is injective, and the branch ranges are disjoint, so $h$ is injective. Every $z\ge0$ has preimage $2z$, and every $z<0$ has preimage $-2z-1\in\mathbb N$, so it is onto.
parts.rubric: 1 formula and integer outputs; 1 injection including disjoint ranges; 1 preimages for all integers.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Write T or F for each statement. No justification is required. Each item is worth 1 point.\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]\item $\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ is finite.\item The nonnegative even integers are countably infinite.\item The set of binary sequences with exactly six ones is countably infinite.\item $\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)$ is countably infinite.\item Every proper subset of a finite set has smaller cardinality.\item An uncountable set can be listed by the natural numbers with no omissions.\item The set of all finite computer programs is uncountable.\end{enumerate}
parts.solution: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]\item \textbf{F}. No finite natural-number list contains every natural number.\item \textbf{T}. The map $n\mapsto2n$ is a bijection from $\mathbb N$.\item \textbf{T}. Encode by six increasing positions and enumerate finite layers; varying the last position gives infinitely many sequences.\item \textbf{T}. Filter an enumeration of rationals; $1/(n+2)$ gives infinitely many members.\item \textbf{T}. A proper subset omits at least one distinct element of the finite set.\item \textbf{F}. Such a listing would make it countable.\item \textbf{F}. Programs are finite strings over a finite alphabet and can be ordered by length.\end{enumerate}
